title: His trombone style compared with other trombonists
summary: He says he never criticizes other trombonists, describes his range and mixed influences, and praises Vic Dickerson and Jack Teagarden.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: So you played mostly with the reading bands, that were you?
Oh yeah, yeah. Up until recently. I had to. Well, no, I'm glad you asked this question. Now I'm supposed to play tonight. Now I've heard Louie Nelson.

Now I want you to understand me. I never knock another musician. I mean it doesn't do you any good. It hurts you, not the musician. Then you make an enemy for life. Now I've heard Louie Nelson, I've heard this other Jim Robinson, and I've heard some trombone players here. Now where Danny Barker was playing, there's a trombone player there. He sounded pretty good in his German fellow. He sounded nice. And I'm not fine with Jim Robinson, nobody. They're friends of mine. All I'm saying is that I had to get away from the style of Nelson and Jim Robinson, because the fellows began to tell me as the music progressed, say in the 50s, going to sections and everything, and the solo, well they didn't want me to play bop, bop, bop, bop, bop, bop, bop, bop, bop. But I can. I'll say, not brag, I'm flexible. See I can play most of any category, because I've had training, Marquette Extension University, for a theory and harmony and stuff like that, you understand? I've been in the theater, I've been in the brass band, and I've been in the bands when they had sections when I had to take and blend with the two other trombones. So I've taken a little bit from here, a little bit from there, a little bit from there. See? I'm not saying the way I play is just strictly my style. I'm saying that I gather something from Rob Palmer, I've got something from Dutre, and even a little touch of Tea Gardens, and other Fred Robinson. You know, people sound good to me when I go home and practice. It's a mixture, you see what I'm talking about? And so, I can play Dixieland, you understand? As you'll hear me, I can play Dixieland, but when it comes to my solo, then I'm a little more modern than Roberson and the other fellas, you understand what I'm talking about? I'm more on the order, the German boy and the other fellas, you understand? Not too high. My range is Bb and sometimes C, but not way up there. I can play there as far as F, but I don't find it necessary. You see, I don't find it necessary. I can get plenty out of, from Bb, which is just occasionally Ab. And that G and that Eb and that, I can get plenty out of, right down there. It's plenty. And you have some body. You see? But the high notes are not necessary.
No. But it's low instrument, right?

Now I like the way Vic Dickerson plays. See now he plays up there you know. He's smooth. He has a nice intonation. You see what I'm talking about? I love the way Jack Teagarden sang and played, you understand? I met Jack in Texas years ago. I always liked the way he played. I liked the way he sang just like he played. So I've taken a little bit from a lot of fellas. I'm not all that original. But my background and the foundation is New Orleans. I can make those glisters as you'll hear me. You know when I was singing. So what did he say? So I can play that. Because I started playing that way. And as you find on these records, you see, you'll find that I play a lot of different sounds than I did on this record.
